content.text: Mean rate: a worked example
Mean rate is the average over a chosen time interval. mean rate = gas volume ÷ time
Volume produced = 36 − 0 = 36 cm³
Time taken = 30 − 0 = 30 s
Mean rate = 36 ÷ 30 = 1.2 cm³/s

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: At zero seconds the gas volume is zero cubic centimetres; at 30 seconds it is 36 cubic centimetres.

content.text: Calculate a mean rate
A reaction produces 0 cm³ at 0 s and 48 cm³ at 40 s. Calculate its mean rate.
A second reaction produces 0 cm³ at 0 s and 48 cm³ at 60 s. Calculate its mean rate.
Which reaction is faster on average? Use your results.
Write the calculation and the unit.
Why does concentration matter?
A higher concentration means more acid particles in the same volume.
Acid particles collide with the magnesium surface more often.
More collisions succeed each second, so the rate increases.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Equal-sized panels compare eight and sixteen acid particles above identical magnesium surfaces, with equal liquid volumes and equally long movement arrows.

content.text: More particles, not faster particles
Doubling concentration at the same temperature does not make particles move faster.
Compare equal volumes of dilute and concentrated acid at 20°C with identical magnesium surfaces; the concentrated acid has twice as many acid particles.
Successful collisions need enough energy to react.
Both samples have the same distribution of particle speeds. More particles mean more collisions each second, not more energy per collision.
Choose the best explanation
Why does more concentrated acid react faster with magnesium at the same temperature?
A
Acid particles move faster.
B
The magnesium gains a larger surface.
C
Successful collisions happen more often.
D
Each collision has more energy.
Investigate concentration
Use 25 cm³ of acid; change its concentration.
Keep magnesium mass, surface area and temperature the same.
Add magnesium, seal promptly and start timing.
Record gas every 10 s; repeat each test three times.

content.text: Calculate each mean rate from 0–20 s. Which used stronger acid? Explain why both finish at 40 cm³.
Can we trust this conclusion?
Test X: 0.5 mol/dm³ acid, 0.04 g magnesium, 20°C. Test Y: 1.0 mol/dm³ acid, 0.08 g magnesium, 30°C. Y reacts faster. Can concentration alone explain this?
Redesign these tests to isolate the effect of concentration.
Stretch: with mass, surface area and temperature fixed, explain why higher concentration increases the number of successful collisions each second.
Evaluate the claim and improve the test.
